name: Double cleansing

lead: Double cleansing means washing the face twice in the evening: first with an oil, balm or micellar water, then with a water-based cleanser. People use it to remove sunscreen, makeup and oil completely, leaving pores cleaner and skin looking clearer. It comes from Korean and Japanese beauty routines.

The oil step dissolves oil-soluble residues such as water-resistant sunscreen and sebum, and the water-based step removes what remains and rinses the oil away. No published trial has tested the routine itself, and general dermatology references describe cleansing as routine acne care.

paras: It is done as an evening step, oil or balm massaged onto dry skin and rinsed, then a gentle foaming or gel cleanser. People who wear sunscreen or makeup daily tend to use it most.
Risks are mild: irritation from over-washing and, for some people, breakouts from comedogenic oils in the first step. Some oils are described as pore-clogging for some skin types.

news.title: Double cleansing benefits the beauty industry , not consumers | Skincare
6 Steps to Glass Skin , According to K - Beauty Experts

angle.text: An oil cleanser followed by a water-based one removes sunscreen, makeup and sebum that a single wash can leave behind, so pores stay cleaner and skin looks clearer. The routine comes from Korean and Japanese beauty practice.

lead: Double cleansing is a two-step facial washing routine in which an oil-based or other lipid-soluble cleanser (a cleansing oil, balm or micellar water) is applied first, followed by a water-based cleanser that is emulsified with water and rinsed off.[1] It is associated with Korean and Japanese beauty routines and is described in looksmaxxing and skincare communities as an evening step used to remove sunscreen, makeup and sebum so that skin looks clearer and smoother.[1][2][3]

Proponents say the first step dissolves oil-soluble residues such as water-resistant sunscreen and waterproof makeup that a single water-based wash may leave behind, and that the second step removes the remaining oil and water-soluble debris.[1] Wikipedia's K-beauty article describes a dual cleansing ritual with oil- and water-based products as the opening of the Korean routine, which averages ten steps.[3]

Dermatologists quoted in general references describe cleansing as a routine part of acne care but note that evidence for specific cleansing practices is limited.[4] No published clinical trial has tested double cleansing as a regimen for acne or appearance.
infobox: Water-resistant sunscreen, waterproof makeup, sebum, pollution particles[1]
None found for the routine itself

paras: In the commonly described form, a lipid-soluble cleanser such as a cleansing oil, balm or micellar water is massaged onto dry skin, the face may be splashed with water, and a water-based cleanser is then lathered or emulsified and rinsed off thoroughly.[1] The first step is intended for residues that resist water, including water-resistant sunscreen, long-wear makeup, excess sebum and particulate pollution.[1]

Cleansing is described as the first step in a skincare routine, followed by toner and moisturizer, and it can help prevent clogged pores, dullness and shine and may help with acne.[1][4] Some cleansers add moisturizing, exfoliating, brightening or anti-acne ingredients, and fragrance-free versions are often recommended by dermatologists for sensitive skin.[1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, explains oil cleansing with the 'like dissolves like' principle: oils dissolve oil-soluble debris when massaged into dry skin, and adding water emulsifies the mixture so it rinses off. The page adds that oils resemble sebum and may spare the skin's lipid barrier compared with harsh surfactant cleansers, while noting that direct research is limited.[2]

Wikipedia contrasts facial cleansers with alkaline bar soap, which has a pH of about 9 to 10 compared with about 4.7 for healthy skin, and says this may favour bacterial overgrowth and worsen acne, though it marks some of those claims as needing citations.[1]

The first step grows out of long-standing oil cleansing practices. Grokipedia cites castor, sesame and moringa oil use in ancient Egypt, Ayurvedic oil massage, and camellia (tsubaki) oil in Edo-period Japan, and says online forums spread do-it-yourself oil-cleansing blends in the early 2000s, with a detailed guide circulating on Acne.org around 2007.[2] It dates DHC's Deep Cleansing Oil to 1997 in Japan, with international spread in the 2000s, and says Korean beauty popularised oil cleansing in the 2010s as the first step of double cleansing, with influencers such as Michelle Phan promoting it.[2]

Wikipedia's K-beauty article describes the Korean regimen as starting with a dual cleansing ritual followed by sheet masks, essences, serums and moisturizers, and reports that Mintel data attribute about 68 percent of skincare launches to South Korea and that the 2014 drama My Love from the Star was reported to lift skincare sales up to 75 percent.[3] It also says men are increasingly participating in the market while the focus remains on women.[3] Both K-beauty and oil-cleansing articles carry sourcing caveats.[2][3]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and skincare communities
paras: In style- and skin-focused communities it is typically presented as an evening routine layered with other steps (toner, actives, moisturiser), and is often discussed alongside the oil cleansing method and skin cycling. Practitioners usually describe it as a way to keep skin clear of sunscreen and sebum build-up without relying on a single harsh wash.

General references on facial cleansers state that cleansing can help remove oil and debris, and that many cleanser claims, such as effects on pore clogging or oil production, are insufficiently sourced.[1] A broader skincare overview notes that evidence for best cleansing practices is limited.[4]

A questionnaire study of 539 Korean patients with acne examined how cosmetics use relates to acne, but it did not test double cleansing as an intervention.[5] The term 'double-cleansing' also appears in a 2024 retrospective review of chlorhexidine skin preparation before surgery in neonatal intensive care, which concerns a different, antiseptic procedure.[6]

Reported concerns are generally the same as for any cleansing: over-washing or aggressive scrubbing can irritate skin and impair the skin barrier.[4] Grokipedia says some first-step oils, coconut oil in particular, may clog pores in acne-prone skin, that essential-oil additives such as tea tree or lavender are common sensitisers, and that people with active skin infections or rosacea are advised to consult a dermatologist; the page flags that some of its supporting citations are weak.[2]

No studies found. The routine itself has not been tested in published trials; research is limited to broader work on cosmetics use and acne, such as an observational questionnaire study in Korean acne patients.[5]

lore.intro: Double cleansing is discussed in skincare-adjacent looksmaxxing spaces as a standard evening routine, usually without controlled evidence either way.[1]

claims.claim: Cleansing twice, oil first, removes sunscreen and sebum that one wash leaves behind.
Double cleansing keeps pores clear and helps acne-prone skin.
Oil cleansers are gentler on the skin barrier than foaming cleansers.

timeline.event: DHC's Deep Cleansing Oil launches in Japan, per Grokipedia.[2]
